# Three Penn State researchers win 2020 Rustum and Della Roy Awards

![Image 1: Three different images of three young men, one outdoors and two posed in suits](https://psu-gatsby-files-prod.s3.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/styles/4_3_1500w/public/Roy%20Award%20Winners.png?h=9952680c&itok=1Bwu3Brk)

The 2020 Rustum and Della Roy Innovation in Materials Research Award winners are, from left to right, Benjamin C. Steimle, Saptarshi Das, and Kosuke Tsuji.Credit: Penn State. [Creative Commons](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/4.0/)

Expand

December 2, 2020

UNIVERSITY PARK, Pa. — The Materials Research Institute (MRI) has announced the three winners of the 2020 [Rustum and Della Roy Innovation in Materials Research Award](https://www.mri.psu.edu/mri/events/innovation-materials-research-award).

The award recognizes interdisciplinary materials research at Penn State which yields innovative and unexpected results and is given annually to two graduate students and one postdoctoral researcher or junior faculty member. This year’s winners include Saptarshi Das, assistant professor of engineering science and mechanics; Benjamin C. Steimle, doctoral student in materials chemistry; and Kosuke Tsuji, graduate student in material science and engineering.

**Saptarshi Das**

[Das’](https://www.mri.psu.edu/das-saptarshi) area of expertise is design and experimental demonstration of novel nanodevices based on 2D materials, which consist of a single layer of atoms, for sensing, computing, storage and security. His lab’s vision is to pioneer a new multidisciplinary area of science he refers to as biomimetic sensing and neuromorphic computing.

This work is inspired by how animal brains are structured to enable the types of sensory computations needed for the species to survive in resource-constrained environments. The overall goal is to create biomimetic sensing devices to deploy in remote locations such as deep inside the oceans for aquatic research, unstable geological areas for tectonic and volcanic monitoring, infrastructure sites for various sensing needs, and inside human and animal bodies for health monitoring and treatment.

“Energy efficiency is the key towards the sustainable development of modern societies in the emerging era of Internet of Things, where billions of interconnected sensors will enrich human experience,” Das said. “Our research aids towards such endeavors deriving inspiration from the natural world.”

**Benjamin Steimle**

Steimle works in the field of inorganic nanoparticle synthesis, where he develops new ways to make inorganic nanoparticles, objects that have dimensions approximately 1,000 times smaller than the width of human hair. He is part of a collaborative team in the [lab of Raymond Schaak](https://sites.psu.edu/rayschaak/), DuPont Professor of Materials Chemistry and professor of chemical engineering, that focuses on forming general design guidelines to synthesize nanoparticles that contain multiple connections between two or more nanoscale crystals.

Steimle’s work has enabled his lab to make some of the most complex nanoparticles in existence, and further the understanding of synthetic capabilities at the nanoscale.

“My research has enabled the synthesis of multicomponent nanoparticles that couldn’t have been imagined even at the beginning of my thesis work four years ago,” Steimle said. “Our long-term hope is that we can start to explore the real-world relevance of our syntheses through collaborations with chemists, engineers and material scientists.”

**Kosuke Tsuji**

Tsuji’s research focuses on cold sintering, a sintering technique developed by Clive Randall, MRI director, which enables many types of ceramics to be solidified at very low temperatures, much lower than traditional sintering methods. Working in Randall’s lab, Tsuji is part of a team working on cold sintering of ceramic materials used in most electronics components, such as cell phones and computers.

“It may be possible to reduce electrical energy and CO2 emissions by lowering the processing temperature, or to replace expensive metals with common base metals to make electrodes,” Tsuji said. “We are also currently working on synthesizing new types of ceramic-based composites and exploring new functionalities that could not be achieved with traditional approaches.”

Winning the Roy Award has an added, unique meaning to Tsuji.

“I'm sincerely honored to receive this award because the key concept of this work is related to some early work of Professor Della Roy, one of the people the award is named after, that was [published in 1973 in the Journal of Crystal Growth](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0022024873900122),” Tsuji said.

The prestigious award was created by a gift from Della and her late husband Rustum Roy, who are both alumni of Penn State’s College of Earth and Mineral Sciences and long-serving faculty in the college.

“I'm sincerely honored to receive this award because the key concept of this work is related to some early work of Professor Della Roy, one of the people the award is named after, that was [published in 1973 in the Journal of Crystal Growth](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0022024873900122),” Tsuji said.

The prestigious award was created by a gift from Della and her late husband Rustum Roy, who are both alumni of Penn State’s College of Earth and Mineral Sciences and long-serving faculty in the college.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Indian born American physicist (1924–2010)

**Rustum Roy** (July 3, 1924 – August 26, 2010) was a [physicist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physicist "Physicist"), born in India, who became a professor at [Pennsylvania State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_State_University "Pennsylvania State University") and was a leader in [materials research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Materials_research "Materials research"). As an advocate for [interdisciplinarity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interdisciplinarity "Interdisciplinarity"), he initiated a movement of [materials research societies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Materials_research_societies "Materials research societies") and, outside of his multiple areas of scientific and engineering expertise, wrote impassioned pleas about the need for a fusion of [religion and science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religion_and_science "Religion and science") and humanistic causes.

Later in life he held visiting professorships in [materials science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Materials_science "Materials science") at [Arizona State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arizona_State_University "Arizona State University"), and in medicine at the [University of Arizona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Arizona "University of Arizona").

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rustum_Roy&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Roy was born in [Ranchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ranchi "Ranchi"), [Bihar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bihar "Bihar") Province, [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India"), the son of Narenda Kumar and Rajkumari Roy.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rustum_Roy#cite_note-CeramObit-1)

Rustum took a Cambridge School Certificate from [Saint Paul's School Darjeeling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul's_School,_Darjeeling "St. Paul's School, Darjeeling"). Rustum studied [physical chemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physical_chemistry "Physical chemistry") at [Patna University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patna_University "Patna University"), gaining his bachelor's degree in 1942 and master's degree in 1944. The following year he began study at [Pennsylvania State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_State_University "Pennsylvania State University") and earned his Ph.D. in [engineering ceramics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engineering_ceramics "Engineering ceramics") in 1948.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rustum_Roy#cite_note-SS&YI-2)

Rustum Roy married fellow materials scientist [Della Marie Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Della_Roy "Della Roy") on June 8 that year.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rustum_Roy#cite_note-CeramObit-1)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rustum_Roy&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

In 1962 he was named the first director of the Materials Research Laboratory at Penn State.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rustum_Roy#cite_note-SS&YI-2) He edited the _Proceedings_[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rustum_Roy#cite_note-3) of a 1968 Conference on the chemistry of [silicon carbide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_carbide "Silicon carbide"). The next year a national colloquy was held on [materials science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Materials_science "Materials science") in the United States for which Roy edited the _Proceedings_.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rustum_Roy#cite_note-4) In 1973 he edited the _Proceedings_[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rustum_Roy#cite_note-5) of a conference on [phase transitions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phase_transition "Phase transition") and their applications.

In 1974 Roy and Olaf Müller published _The Major Ternary Structural Families_ with Springer-Verlag, which described the principal [crystal structures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystal_structure "Crystal structure") of [ternary compounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ternary_compound "Ternary compound"). The book received two brief reviews in materials trade journals. A cement journal reviewer said it would be "Useful to the practicing materials researcher, whether in industry or university, as well as the non-specialist who needs to become informed about particular materials."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rustum_Roy#cite_note-6) A chemist writing for mineral processing readers, described its depth:

The structural descriptions are at times too brief but the chapters contain valuable information such as compositional structure field maps (radius A vs. radius B), figures of unit cells or the polyhedral arrangements in some common structures, phase diagrams (P vs. T, or P vs. [ionic radius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ionic_radius "Ionic radius")), structural relationships, and phase transition data.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rustum_Roy#cite_note-7)
By 1991 he was a spokesperson for the movement and his lecture "New Materials: Fountainhead for New Technologies and New Science" was published by [National Academy Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Academy_Press "National Academy Press").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rustum_Roy#cite_note-8) Roy presented the lecture to learned audiences in Washington, D.C.; Tokyo, Japan; New Delhi, Stockholm, Copenhagen, and London in 1991 and 92. He made the case for linking a technical need to investigative effort, which he terms "technology traction", noting that the method is productive and cost-effective in comparison to science conducted with other purposes.

Rustum Roy was referred to as "[o]ne of the legends of materials science" at the time of his death.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rustum_Roy#cite_note-CeramObit-1)

Roy was elected as a member of the U.S. [National Academy of Engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Academy_of_Engineering "National Academy of Engineering") in 1973.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rustum_Roy#cite_note-NAEelect-9)

## Other interests

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rustum_Roy&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Other interests")]

### Academic freedom

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rustum_Roy&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Academic freedom")]

In 1953, Roy wrote a letter to _[Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life\_(magazine) "Life (magazine)")_ magazine in response to the essay "Is Academic Freedom in Danger?" by [Whittaker Chambers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whittaker_Chambers "Whittaker Chambers"), stating:

> Sirs:   
>  Chambers neglects to note that since people rarely read Congressional Records, they get their News more by headlines and the tenor of the times. Thus, most professors "know" or "feel" it is safer today to keep your mouth shut, and, if you open it, not to support any liberal or leftish views. Let Chambers continue to remind us of the very real perils of the Communist left. Fanatical preoccupation with self-preservation will lead to loss of more valuable things, not merely academic freedom, but freedom.   
>  Rustum Roy   
>  Assistant Professor   
>  The Pennsylvania State College   
>  State College, PA[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rustum_Roy#cite_note-Life-10)

### University reform

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rustum_Roy&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: University reform")]

In 1977 Rustum Roy proposed[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rustum_Roy#cite_note-CEN-11) that the "science and engineering activity of a university ... [be organized] primarily around a dozen permanent mission-oriented interdisciplinary laboratories." To reach this conclusion he notes that "universities have been forced into new interdisciplinary patterns not only by the dollar sign but also by the inexorable logic that the real problems of society do not come in discipline-shaped blocks."

The daunting structural inertia of the university did not faze him:

A [human being](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_being "Human being"), that is both a naked ape and a [fallen angel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fallen_angel "Fallen angel"), can manage perhaps to organize the university with both the [ivory tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivory_tower "Ivory tower") and service-station character.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rustum_Roy#cite_note-CEN-11):30

### Health

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rustum_Roy&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Health")]

Roy had no formal medical credentials but was an advocate of integrating science, medicine, and spirituality. In the inaugural issue of the [Journal of Ayurveda and Integrative Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journal_of_Ayurveda_and_Integrative_Medicine "Journal of Ayurveda and Integrative Medicine") Roy contributed the article "Integrative medicine to tackle the problem of chronic diseases". He noted that [chronic illness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chronic_illness "Chronic illness") debilitates the lives of many seniors, and that medical interventions are often futile. He said "little of nothing is being spent on [preventative medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preventative_medicine "Preventative medicine")", and cited the ayurveda concepts of "ahara" concerned with nutrition, and "vihara" with the conduct of life. He noted the exemplary work of [Dean Ornish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dean_Ornish "Dean Ornish") in addressing [coronary artery disease](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coronary_artery_disease "Coronary artery disease") as a hopeful innovation.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rustum_Roy#cite_note-12)

In 2010, close to the end of his life, Roy co-wrote an article in the [Huffington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huffington_Post "Huffington Post") called "The Mythology Of Science-Based Medicine" with nonscientists [Deepak Chopra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deepak_Chopra "Deepak Chopra") and [Larry Dossey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Dossey "Larry Dossey"), which David Gorski characterized as "an exercise that combines cherry-picking, logical fallacies, and whining, raising the last of these almost to an art form."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rustum_Roy#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rustum_Roy#cite_note-14)

## Personal life and death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rustum_Roy&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Personal life and death")]

Roy married [Della Martin Roy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Della_Roy "Della Roy") on June 8, 1948. Their three children are Neill R. Roy (deceased),[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rustum_Roy#cite_note-15) Jeremy R. Roy, and Ronnen A. Roy.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rustum_Roy#cite_note-CeramObit-1)

Roy died on August 26, 2010, at the age of 86.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rustum_Roy#cite_note-16) He was survived by his wife and children.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rustum_Roy#cite_note-CeramObit-1)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Indian born American physicist (1924–2010)

**Rustum Roy** (July 3, 1924 – August 26, 2010) was a [physicist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physicist "Physicist"), born in India, who became a professor at [Pennsylvania State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_State_University "Pennsylvania State University") and was a leader in [materials research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Materials_research "Materials research"). As an advocate for [interdisciplinarity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interdisciplinarity "Interdisciplinarity"), he initiated a movement of [materials research societies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Materials_research_societies "Materials research societies") and, outside of his multiple areas of scientific and engineering expertise, wrote impassioned pleas about the need for a fusion of [religion and science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religion_and_science "Religion and science") and humanistic causes.

Later in life he held visiting professorships in [materials science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Materials_science "Materials science") at [Arizona State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arizona_State_University "Arizona State University"), and in medicine at the [University of Arizona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Arizona "University of Arizona").

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rustum_Roy&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Roy was born in [Ranchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ranchi "Ranchi"), [Bihar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bihar "Bihar") Province, [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India"), the son of Narenda Kumar and Rajkumari Roy.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rustum_Roy#cite_note-CeramObit-1)

Rustum took a Cambridge School Certificate from [Saint Paul's School Darjeeling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul's_School,_Darjeeling "St. Paul's School, Darjeeling"). Rustum studied [physical chemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physical_chemistry "Physical chemistry") at [Patna University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patna_University "Patna University"), gaining his bachelor's degree in 1942 and master's degree in 1944. The following year he began study at [Pennsylvania State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_State_University "Pennsylvania State University") and earned his Ph.D. in [engineering ceramics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engineering_ceramics "Engineering ceramics") in 1948.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rustum_Roy#cite_note-SS&YI-2)

Rustum Roy married fellow materials scientist [Della Marie Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Della_Roy "Della Roy") on June 8 that year.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rustum_Roy#cite_note-CeramObit-1)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rustum_Roy&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

In 1962 he was named the first director of the Materials Research Laboratory at Penn State.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rustum_Roy#cite_note-SS&YI-2) He edited the _Proceedings_[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rustum_Roy#cite_note-3) of a 1968 Conference on the chemistry of [silicon carbide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_carbide "Silicon carbide"). The next year a national colloquy was held on [materials science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Materials_science "Materials science") in the United States for which Roy edited the _Proceedings_.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rustum_Roy#cite_note-4) In 1973 he edited the _Proceedings_[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rustum_Roy#cite_note-5) of a conference on [phase transitions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phase_transition "Phase transition") and their applications.

In 1974 Roy and Olaf Müller published _The Major Ternary Structural Families_ with Springer-Verlag, which described the principal [crystal structures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystal_structure "Crystal structure") of [ternary compounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ternary_compound "Ternary compound"). The book received two brief reviews in materials trade journals. A cement journal reviewer said it would be "Useful to the practicing materials researcher, whether in industry or university, as well as the non-specialist who needs to become informed about particular materials."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rustum_Roy#cite_note-6) A chemist writing for mineral processing readers, described its depth:

The structural descriptions are at times too brief but the chapters contain valuable information such as compositional structure field maps (radius A vs. radius B), figures of unit cells or the polyhedral arrangements in some common structures, phase diagrams (P vs. T, or P vs. [ionic radius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ionic_radius "Ionic radius")), structural relationships, and phase transition data.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rustum_Roy#cite_note-7)
By 1991 he was a spokesperson for the movement and his lecture "New Materials: Fountainhead for New Technologies and New Science" was published by [National Academy Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Academy_Press "National Academy Press").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rustum_Roy#cite_note-8) Roy presented the lecture to learned audiences in Washington, D.C.; Tokyo, Japan; New Delhi, Stockholm, Copenhagen, and London in 1991 and 92. He made the case for linking a technical need to investigative effort, which he terms "technology traction", noting that the method is productive and cost-effective in comparison to science conducted with other purposes.

Rustum Roy was referred to as "[o]ne of the legends of materials science" at the time of his death.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rustum_Roy#cite_note-CeramObit-1)

Roy was elected as a member of the U.S. [National Academy of Engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Academy_of_Engineering "National Academy of Engineering") in 1973.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rustum_Roy#cite_note-NAEelect-9)

## Other interests

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rustum_Roy&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Other interests")]

### Academic freedom

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rustum_Roy&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Academic freedom")]

In 1953, Roy wrote a letter to _[Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life\_(magazine) "Life (magazine)")_ magazine in response to the essay "Is Academic Freedom in Danger?" by [Whittaker Chambers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whittaker_Chambers "Whittaker Chambers"), stating:

> Sirs:   
>  Chambers neglects to note that since people rarely read Congressional Records, they get their News more by headlines and the tenor of the times. Thus, most professors "know" or "feel" it is safer today to keep your mouth shut, and, if you open it, not to support any liberal or leftish views. Let Chambers continue to remind us of the very real perils of the Communist left. Fanatical preoccupation with self-preservation will lead to loss of more valuable things, not merely academic freedom, but freedom.   
>  Rustum Roy   
>  Assistant Professor   
>  The Pennsylvania State College   
>  State College, PA[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rustum_Roy#cite_note-Life-10)

### University reform

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rustum_Roy&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: University reform")]

In 1977 Rustum Roy proposed[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rustum_Roy#cite_note-CEN-11) that the "science and engineering activity of a university ... [be organized] primarily around a dozen permanent mission-oriented interdisciplinary laboratories." To reach this conclusion he notes that "universities have been forced into new interdisciplinary patterns not only by the dollar sign but also by the inexorable logic that the real problems of society do not come in discipline-shaped blocks."

The daunting structural inertia of the university did not faze him:

A [human being](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_being "Human being"), that is both a naked ape and a [fallen angel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fallen_angel "Fallen angel"), can manage perhaps to organize the university with both the [ivory tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivory_tower "Ivory tower") and service-station character.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rustum_Roy#cite_note-CEN-11):30

### Health

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rustum_Roy&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Health")]

Roy had no formal medical credentials but was an advocate of integrating science, medicine, and spirituality. In the inaugural issue of the [Journal of Ayurveda and Integrative Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journal_of_Ayurveda_and_Integrative_Medicine "Journal of Ayurveda and Integrative Medicine") Roy contributed the article "Integrative medicine to tackle the problem of chronic diseases". He noted that [chronic illness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chronic_illness "Chronic illness") debilitates the lives of many seniors, and that medical interventions are often futile. He said "little of nothing is being spent on [preventative medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preventative_medicine "Preventative medicine")", and cited the ayurveda concepts of "ahara" concerned with nutrition, and "vihara" with the conduct of life. He noted the exemplary work of [Dean Ornish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dean_Ornish "Dean Ornish") in addressing [coronary artery disease](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coronary_artery_disease "Coronary artery disease") as a hopeful innovation.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rustum_Roy#cite_note-12)

In 2010, close to the end of his life, Roy co-wrote an article in the [Huffington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huffington_Post "Huffington Post") called "The Mythology Of Science-Based Medicine" with nonscientists [Deepak Chopra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deepak_Chopra "Deepak Chopra") and [Larry Dossey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Dossey "Larry Dossey"), which David Gorski characterized as "an exercise that combines cherry-picking, logical fallacies, and whining, raising the last of these almost to an art form."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rustum_Roy#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rustum_Roy#cite_note-14)

## Personal life and death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rustum_Roy&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Personal life and death")]

Roy married [Della Martin Roy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Della_Roy "Della Roy") on June 8, 1948. Their three children are Neill R. Roy (deceased),[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rustum_Roy#cite_note-15) Jeremy R. Roy, and Ronnen A. Roy.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rustum_Roy#cite_note-CeramObit-1)

Roy died on August 26, 2010, at the age of 86.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rustum_Roy#cite_note-16) He was survived by his wife and children.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rustum_Roy#cite_note-CeramObit-1)

**Hoboken** ([/ˈ h oʊ b oʊ k ən/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")[_HOH-boh-kən_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key");[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-Lippincott-19)[Unami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unami_language "Unami language"): _Hupokàn_)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-20) is a [city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_(New_Jersey) "City (New Jersey)") in [Hudson County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson_County,_New_Jersey "Hudson County, New Jersey") in the [U.S. state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._state "U.S. state") of [New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jersey "New Jersey"). Hoboken is part of the [New York metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_metropolitan_area "New York metropolitan area") and is the site of [Hoboken Terminal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken_Terminal "Hoboken Terminal"), a major [transportation hub](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_hub "Transportation hub"). As of the [2020 United States census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census "2020 United States census"), the city's population was 60,419,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-Census2020-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-LWD2020-10) an increase of 10,414 (+20.8%) from the [2010 census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_United_States_census "2010 United States census") count of 50,005,[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-Census2010-21) which in turn reflected an increase of 11,428 (+29.6%) from the 38,577 counted in the [2000 census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_United_States_census "2000 United States census").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-22) The [Census Bureau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Census_Bureau "United States Census Bureau")'s [Population Estimates Program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Population_Estimates_Program "Population Estimates Program") calculated a population of 59,149 for 2024.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-PopEst-11) With more than 42,400 inhabitants per square mile (16,400/km 2) in data from the 2010 census, Hoboken was ranked as the third-most [densely populated municipality in the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_cities_by_population_density "List of United States cities by population density") among cities with a population above 50,000.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-23) In the 2020 census, the city's population density climbed to more than 48,300 inhabitants per square mile (18,600/km 2) of land, ranked fourth in the county behind [Guttenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guttenberg,_New_Jersey "Guttenberg, New Jersey"), [Union City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_City,_New_Jersey "Union City, New Jersey") and [West New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_New_York,_New_Jersey "West New York, New Jersey"), all of which are in Hudson County.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-Census2020-9)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-24)

Hoboken was first settled by Europeans as part of the [Pavonia, New Netherland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pavonia,_New_Netherland "Pavonia, New Netherland") colony in the 17th century. During the early 19th century, the city was developed by [Colonel John Stevens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Stevens_(inventor,_born_1749) "John Stevens (inventor, born 1749)"), first as a resort and later as a residential neighborhood. Originally part of [Bergen Township](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bergen_Township,_New_Jersey_(1661%E2%80%931862) "Bergen Township, New Jersey (1661–1862)") and later [North Bergen Township](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Bergen,_New_Jersey "North Bergen, New Jersey"), it became a separate township in 1849 and was incorporated as a city in 1855. Hoboken is the location of the first recorded game of [baseball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baseball "Baseball") and of the [Stevens Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stevens_Institute_of_Technology "Stevens Institute of Technology"), one of the oldest technological universities in the United States.

It is also known as the birthplace and hometown of the world-famous singer and actor [Frank Sinatra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Sinatra "Frank Sinatra") (1915–1998); various streets and parks in the city have been named after him.

Located on the [Hudson Waterfront](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson_Waterfront "Hudson Waterfront"), the city was an integral part of the [Port of New York and New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_of_New_York_and_New_Jersey "Port of New York and New Jersey") and was home to major industries for most of the 20th century. The character of the city has changed from an artsy industrial vibe from the days when Maxwell House coffee, Lipton tea, Hostess Cupcakes, and [Wonder Bread](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wonder_Bread "Wonder Bread") called Hoboken home, to one of trendy shops and expensive condominiums.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-25) It was ranked 2nd in [Niche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niche.com "Niche.com")'s "2019 Best Places to Live in Hudson County" list,[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-26) and 1st in 2022.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-27)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hoboken,_New_Jersey&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Etymology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hoboken,_New_Jersey&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Etymology")]

The name Hoboken was chosen by Colonel [John Stevens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Stevens_(inventor,_born_1749) "John Stevens (inventor, born 1749)") when he bought land on a part of which the city still sits. The [Lenape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lenape "Lenape"), later called Delaware Indian tribe of [Native Americans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_Americans_in_the_United_States "Native Americans in the United States"), referred to the area as the "land of the tobacco pipe", most likely to refer to the [soapstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soapstone "Soapstone") collected there to carve [tobacco pipes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tobacco_pipe "Tobacco pipe"), and used a phrase that became "Hopoghan Hackingh".[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-HobokenMuseum-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-30) Like [Weehawken](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weehawken,_New_Jersey "Weehawken, New Jersey"), its neighbor to the north, as well as [Communipaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communipaw "Communipaw") and [Harsimus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harsimus "Harsimus") to the south, Hoboken had many variations in the folks-tongue. _Hoebuck_, old Dutch for high bluff, and likely referring to Castle Point, the district of the city highest above sea level, was used during the colonial era, and was later spelled as _Hobuck_,[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-31)_Hobock_,[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-32)_Hobuk_[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-33) and _Hoboocken_.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-34) However, in the nineteenth century, the name was changed to Hoboken, influenced by [Flemish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flemish_people "Flemish people") immigrants, and a [folk etymology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_etymology "Folk etymology") had emerged, linking the town of Hoboken to the similarly named [Hoboken](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_Antwerp "Hoboken, Antwerp") district of [Antwerp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antwerp "Antwerp").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-35)

Hoboken has been nicknamed the Mile Square City,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-MileSquare-1) but it actually occupies about 1.25 sq mi (3.2 km 2) of land.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-CensusArea-2) During the late 19th/early 20th century the population and culture of Hoboken was dominated by [German language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_language "German language") speakers who sometimes called it "Little Bremen", many of whom are buried in [Hoboken Cemetery, North Bergen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken_Cemetery,_North_Bergen "Hoboken Cemetery, North Bergen").[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-37)

### Early-European arrival and colonial period

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hoboken,_New_Jersey&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Early-European arrival and colonial period")]

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8c/HudsonRiverJerseyCity1890.jpg/250px-HudsonRiverJerseyCity1890.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:HudsonRiverJerseyCity1890.jpg)

The [Hudson River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson_River "Hudson River") during the 1880s offshore from Hoboken and [Jersey City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jersey_City,_New_Jersey "Jersey City, New Jersey")

Hoboken was originally an island which was surrounded by the [Hudson River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson_River "Hudson River") on the east and tidal lands at the foot of the [New Jersey Palisades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jersey_Palisades "New Jersey Palisades") on the west. It was a seasonal campsite in the territory of the [Hackensack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hackensack_(Native_Americans) "Hackensack (Native Americans)"), a [phratry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phratry "Phratry") of the [Lenni Lenape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lenape "Lenape"), who used the serpentine rock found there to carve pipes.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-HobokenMuseum-28)

The first recorded European to lay claim to the area was [Henry Hudson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Hudson "Henry Hudson"), an Englishman sailing for the [Dutch East India Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_East_India_Company "Dutch East India Company"), who anchored his ship the _[Halve Maen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halve\_Maen "Halve Maen")_ (_Half Moon_) at [Weehawken Cove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weehawken_Cove "Weehawken Cove") on October 2, 1609.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-Hoboken_Museum-38) An entry made in the journal of Hudson's mate, Robert Juet, on that date, is the earliest known reference to the area today known as Hoboken, and would be the last known such reference until twenty years later.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-39) Soon after the area became part of the province of [New Netherland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Netherland "New Netherland").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In 1630, [Michael Reyniersz Pauw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Reyniersz_Pauw "Michael Reyniersz Pauw"), a burgemeester (mayor) of [Amsterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsterdam "Amsterdam") and a director of the [Dutch West India Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_West_India_Company "Dutch West India Company"), received a land grant as [patroon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patroon "Patroon") on the condition that he would plant a colony of not fewer than fifty persons within four years on the west bank of what had been named the [North River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_River_(New_York-New_Jersey) "North River (New York-New Jersey)"). Three Lenape sold the land that became Hoboken and part of Jersey City for 80 fathoms (146 m) of [wampum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wampum "Wampum"), 20 fathoms (37 m) of cloth, 12 kettles, six guns, two blankets, one double kettle, and half a barrel of beer.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-Hoboken_Museum-38) These transactions, variously dated as July 12, 1630 and November 22, 1630, represent the earliest known conveyance for the area. Pauw, whose Latinized name is [Pavonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pavonia,_New_Netherland "Pavonia, New Netherland"), failed to settle the land, and he was obliged to sell his holdings back to the company in 1633.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

It was later acquired by Hendrick Van Vorst, who leased part of the land to Aert Van Putten, a farmer. In 1643, north of what would be later known as Castle Point, Van Putten built a house and a brewery, North America's first. In [series of Indian and Dutch raids and reprisals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kieft's_War "Kieft's War"), Van Putten was killed and his buildings destroyed, and all residents of Pavonia, as the colony was then known, were ordered back to New Amsterdam.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-40)

In 1664, the English took possession of [New Amsterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Amsterdam "New Amsterdam") with little to no resistance, and in 1668 they confirmed a previous land patent by Nicolas Verlett. In 1674–1675, the area became part of [East Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Jersey "East Jersey"), and the province was divided into four administrative districts, Hoboken becoming part of [Bergen County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bergen_County,_New_Jersey "Bergen County, New Jersey"), where it remained until the creation of [Hudson County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson_County,_New_Jersey "Hudson County, New Jersey") on February 22, 1840. English-speaking settlers (some relocating from New England) interspersed with the Dutch, but it remained sparsely populated and agrarian.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Eventually, the land came into the possession of William [Bayard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayard_family "Bayard family"), who originally supported the revolutionary cause, but became a [Loyalist Tory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loyalist_(American_Revolution) "Loyalist (American Revolution)") after the fall of New York in 1776 when the city and surrounding areas, including the west bank of the renamed Hudson River, were occupied by the British. At the end of the [Revolutionary War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolutionary_War "American Revolutionary War"), Bayard's property was confiscated by the Revolutionary Government of New Jersey. In 1784, the land described as "William Bayard's farm at Hoebuck" was bought at auction by Colonel [John Stevens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Stevens_(inventor,_born_1749) "John Stevens (inventor, born 1749)") for £18,360 (then $90,000).[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-Hoboken_Museum-38)

### 19th century

In the early 19th century, Colonel [John Stevens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Stevens_(inventor,_born_1749) "John Stevens (inventor, born 1749)") developed the waterfront as a resort for Manhattanites.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-41) On October 11, 1811, Stevens' ship the _Juliana_, began to operate as a [ferry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferry "Ferry") between Manhattan and Hoboken, making it the world's first commercial steam ferry.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-42) In 1825, he designed and built a [steam locomotive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steam_locomotive "Steam locomotive") capable of hauling several passenger cars at his estate.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-43)[Sybil's Cave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sybil's_Cave "Sybil's Cave"), a cave with a natural spring, was opened in 1832 and visitors came to pay a penny for a glass of water from the cave which was said to have medicinal powers.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-44) In 1841, the cave became a legend, when [Edgar Allan Poe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgar_Allan_Poe "Edgar Allan Poe") wrote "[The Mystery of Marie Roget](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mystery_of_Marie_Roget "The Mystery of Marie Roget")" about an event that took place there.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-45) The cave was closed in the late 1880s after the water was found to be contaminated, and it was shut and in the 1930s and filled with concrete, before it was reopened in 2008.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-46) Before his death in 1838, Stevens founded the [Hoboken Land and Improvement Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken_Land_and_Improvement_Company_Building "Hoboken Land and Improvement Company Building"), which laid out a regular system of streets, blocks and lots, constructed housing, and developed manufacturing sites. In general, the housing consisted of masonry row houses of three to five stories, some of which survive to the present day, as does the street grid.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-47)

Hoboken was originally formed as a [township](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Township_(New_Jersey) "Township (New Jersey)") on April 9, 1849, from portions of [North Bergen Township](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Bergen,_New_Jersey "North Bergen, New Jersey"). As the town grew in population and employment, many of Hoboken's residents saw a need to incorporate as a full-fledged city, and in a referendum held on March 29, 1855, ratified an Act of the [New Jersey Legislature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jersey_Legislature "New Jersey Legislature") signed the previous day, and the City of Hoboken was born.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-Story-48) In the subsequent election, Cornelius V. Clickener became [Hoboken's first mayor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_Hoboken,_New_Jersey "Mayor of Hoboken, New Jersey"). On March 15, 1859, the Township of Weehawken was created from portions of Hoboken and North Bergen Township.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-Story-48)

Based on a bequest from [Edwin A. Stevens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_A._Stevens "Edwin A. Stevens"), [Stevens Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stevens_Institute_of_Technology "Stevens Institute of Technology") was founded at [Castle Point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_Point_(Hoboken) "Castle Point (Hoboken)") in 1870, at the site of the [Stevens family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stevens_family "Stevens family")'s former estate, as the nation's first [mechanical engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mechanical_engineering "Mechanical engineering") college.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-History-49)

By the late 19th century, shipping lines were using Hoboken as a terminal port, and the [Delaware, Lackawanna and Western Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delaware,_Lackawanna_and_Western_Railroad "Delaware, Lackawanna and Western Railroad") (later the [Erie Lackawanna Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erie_Lackawanna_Railroad "Erie Lackawanna Railroad")) developed a railroad terminal at the waterfront, with the present [NJ Transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NJ_Transit "NJ Transit") terminal designed by architect [Kenneth Murchison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_MacKenzie_Murchison "Kenneth MacKenzie Murchison") constructed in 1907.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-50) It was also during this time that German immigrants, who had been settling in town during most of the century, became the predominant population group in the city, at least partially due to its being a major destination port of the [Hamburg America Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamburg_America_Line "Hamburg America Line"), though anti-German sentiment during World War I led to a rapid decline in the German community.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-51) In addition to the primary industry of shipbuilding, Hoboken became home to [Keuffel and Esser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keuffel_and_Esser "Keuffel and Esser")'s three-story factory and in 1884, to Tietjen and Lang Drydock (later [Todd Shipyards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Todd_Shipyards "Todd Shipyards")). Well-known companies that developed a major presence in Hoboken after the turn-of the-century included [Maxwell House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maxwell_House "Maxwell House"), [Lipton Tea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lipton "Lipton"), and [Hostess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hostess_(brand) "Hostess (brand)").[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-52)

#### Birthplace of baseball

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hoboken,_New_Jersey&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Birthplace of baseball")]

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/34/Baseball_at_Elysian_Fields%2C_Hoboken%2C_NJ_in_1866.jpg/250px-Baseball_at_Elysian_Fields%2C_Hoboken%2C_NJ_in_1866.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Baseball_at_Elysian_Fields,_Hoboken,_NJ_in_1866.jpg)

Early baseball game played at [Elysian Fields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elysian_Fields_(Hoboken,_New_Jersey) "Elysian Fields (Hoboken, New Jersey)")

[![Image 26](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c7/1.20.10ElysianFieldsMarkerByLuigiNovi.jpg/250px-1.20.10ElysianFieldsMarkerByLuigiNovi.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1.20.10ElysianFieldsMarkerByLuigiNovi.jpg)

A historic marker stands at the intersection of 11th and Washington Streets, former site of Elysian Fields

The first officially recorded game of [baseball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baseball "Baseball") took place in Hoboken in 1846 between [Knickerbocker Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knickerbocker_Base_Ball_Club_of_New_York "Knickerbocker Base Ball Club of New York") and New York Nine at [Elysian Fields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elysian_Fields,_Hoboken,_New_Jersey "Elysian Fields, Hoboken, New Jersey").[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-53) In 1845, the Knickerbocker Club, which had been founded by [Alexander Cartwright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Cartwright "Alexander Cartwright"), began using Elysian Fields to play [baseball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baseball "Baseball") due to the lack of suitable grounds on [Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan "Manhattan").[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-54) Team members included players of the [St George's Cricket Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_George's_Cricket_Club "St George's Cricket Club"), the brothers [Harry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Wright "Harry Wright") and [George Wright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Wright_(sportsman) "George Wright (sportsman)"), and [Henry Chadwick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Chadwick_(writer) "Henry Chadwick (writer)"), the English-born journalist who coined the term "America's Pastime".[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

By the 1850s, several [Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan "Manhattan")-based members of the [National Association of Base Ball Players](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Association_of_Base_Ball_Players "National Association of Base Ball Players") were using the grounds as their home field while St. George's continued to organize international matches between Canada, England and the United States at the same venue. In 1859, [George Parr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Parr_(cricketer) "George Parr (cricketer)")'s All England Eleven of professional cricketers played the United States XXII at Hoboken, easily defeating the local competition. Sam Wright and his sons Harry and George Wright played on the defeated United States team, a loss which inadvertently encouraged local players to take up baseball. Henry Chadwick believed that baseball and not cricket should become the national pastime after the game drawing the conclusion that amateur American players did not have the leisure time required to develop cricket skills to the high technical level required of professional players. [Harry Wright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Wright "Harry Wright") and [George Wright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Wright_(sportsman) "George Wright (sportsman)") then became two of the first professional baseball players in the United States when Aaron Champion raised funds to found the [Cincinnati Red Stockings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cincinnati_Red_Stockings "Cincinnati Red Stockings") in 1869.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In 1865, the grounds hosted a championship match between the [Mutual Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Mutuals "New York Mutuals") of New York City and the [Atlantic Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn_Atlantics "Brooklyn Atlantics") of [Brooklyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn "Brooklyn") that was attended by an estimated 20,000 fans and captured in the [Currier & Ives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Currier_&_Ives "Currier & Ives")[lithograph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithograph "Lithograph") "The American National Game of Base Ball".[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-55)

With the construction of two significant baseball parks enclosed by fences in [Brooklyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn "Brooklyn"), enabling promoters there to charge admission to games, the prominence of [Elysian Fields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elysian_Fields,_Hoboken,_New_Jersey "Elysian Fields, Hoboken, New Jersey") diminished. In 1868 the leading [Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan "Manhattan") club, [Mutual](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Mutuals "New York Mutuals"), shifted its home games to the [Union Grounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Grounds "Union Grounds") in Brooklyn. In 1880, the founders of the [New York Metropolitans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Metropolitans "New York Metropolitans") and [New York Giants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Giants_(NL) "New York Giants (NL)") finally succeeded in siting a ballpark in Manhattan that became known as the [Polo Grounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polo_Grounds "Polo Grounds").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The _[Brooklyn Eagle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn\_Eagle "Brooklyn Eagle")_ claimed that an unwritten [sundown town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sundown_town "Sundown town") policy prevented African Americans from residing or working there.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-56)

#### World War I

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hoboken,_New_Jersey&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: World War I")]

Further information: [Hoboken Port of Embarkation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken_Port_of_Embarkation "Hoboken Port of Embarkation")

When the U.S. entered [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I"), the [Hamburg-American Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamburg-American_Line "Hamburg-American Line") piers in Hoboken and [New Orleans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans "New Orleans") were taken under [eminent domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eminent_domain "Eminent domain").[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-57) Federal control of the port and anti-German sentiment led to part of the city being placed under martial law, and many German immigrants were forcibly moved to [Ellis Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellis_Island "Ellis Island") or left the city of their own accord.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-58) Hoboken became the major point of embarkation and more than three million soldiers, known as "[doughboys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doughboy "Doughboy")", passed through the city.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-59) Their hope for an early return led to [General Pershing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_J._Pershing "John J. Pershing")'s slogan, "Heaven, Hell or Hoboken... by Christmas."[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-60)

Following the war, [Italians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italians "Italians"), mostly stemming from the [Adriatic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adriatic_Sea "Adriatic Sea") port city of [Molfetta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molfetta "Molfetta"), became the city's major ethnic group, with the [Irish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_ethnicity "Irish ethnicity") also having a strong presence.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-61) While the city experienced the [Great Depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression "Great Depression"), jobs in the ships yards and factories were still available, and the tenements were bustling. Middle-European Jews, mostly German-speaking, also made their way to the city and established small businesses. The [Port Authority of New York and New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Authority_of_New_York_and_New_Jersey "Port Authority of New York and New Jersey"), which was established on April 30, 1921, oversaw the development of the [Holland Tunnel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holland_Tunnel "Holland Tunnel") (completed in 1927) and the [Lincoln Tunnel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lincoln_Tunnel "Lincoln Tunnel") (in 1937), allowing for easier vehicular travel between New Jersey and New York City, bypassing the waterfront.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

#### Post-World War II

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hoboken,_New_Jersey&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Post-World War II")]

The war facilitated economic growth in Hoboken, as the many industries located in the city were crucial to the war effort. As men went off to battle, more women were hired in the factories, some (most notably, [Todd Shipyards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Todd_Shipyards "Todd Shipyards")), offering classes and other incentives to them. Though some returning service men took advantage of GI housing bills, many with strong ethnic and familial ties chose to stay in town. During the 1950s, the economy was still driven by Todd Shipyards, [Maxwell House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maxwell_House "Maxwell House"),[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-62)[Lipton Tea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lipton_Tea "Lipton Tea"), [Hostess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hostess_(brand) "Hostess (brand)") and [Bethlehem Steel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bethlehem_Steel "Bethlehem Steel") and companies with big plants were still not inclined to invest in major infrastructure elsewhere.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

[![Image 29](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/79/Yellow_Flats_03.jpg/250px-Yellow_Flats_03.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Yellow_Flats_03.jpg)

Hoboken historic district

In the 1960s, working pay and conditions began to deteriorate: turn-of-the century housing started to look shabby and feel crowded, shipbuilding was cheaper overseas, and single-story plants surrounded by parking lots made manufacturing and distribution more economical than old brick buildings on congested urban streets. The city appeared to be in the throes of inexorable decline as industries sought (what had been) greener pastures, port operations shifted to larger facilities on [Newark Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newark_Bay "Newark Bay"), and the car, truck and plane displaced the railroad and ship as the transportation modes of choice in the United States. Many Hobokenites headed to the suburbs, often the close by ones in [Bergen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bergen_County,_New_Jersey "Bergen County, New Jersey") and [Passaic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passaic_County,_New_Jersey "Passaic County, New Jersey") Counties, and real-estate values declined. Hoboken sank from its earlier incarnation as a lively port town into a rundown condition and was often included in lists with other New Jersey cities experiencing the same phenomenon, such as [Paterson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paterson,_New_Jersey "Paterson, New Jersey"), [Elizabeth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth,_New_Jersey "Elizabeth, New Jersey"), [Camden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camden,_New_Jersey "Camden, New Jersey"), and neighboring [Jersey City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jersey_City,_New_Jersey "Jersey City, New Jersey").[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-63)

The old economic underpinnings were gone and nothing new seemed to be on the horizon. Attempts were made to stabilize the population by demolishing the so-called slums along River Street and build subsidized middle-income housing at Marineview Plaza, and in midtown, at Church Towers. Heaps of long uncollected garbage and roving packs of semi-wild dogs were not uncommon sights.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-64) Though the city had seen better days, Hoboken was never abandoned. New infusions of immigrants, most notably [Puerto Ricans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puerto_Rican_American "Puerto Rican American"), kept the storefronts open with small businesses and housing stock from being abandoned, but there wasn't much work to be had. Washington Street, commonly called "the avenue", was never boarded up, and the tight-knit neighborhoods remained home to many who were still proud of their city. Stevens remained a premier technology school, Maxwell House kept chugging away, and Bethlehem Steel still housed sailors who were dry-docked on its piers. Italian-Americans and other came back to the "old neighborhood" to shop for delicatessen.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

[![Image 30](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a5/Keuffel_and_Esser_Manufacturing_Complex_Hoboken_November_2021.jpg/250px-Keuffel_and_Esser_Manufacturing_Complex_Hoboken_November_2021.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Keuffel_and_Esser_Manufacturing_Complex_Hoboken_November_2021.jpg)

The [Keuffel and Esser Manufacturing Complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keuffel_and_Esser_Manufacturing_Complex "Keuffel and Esser Manufacturing Complex") was converted into residential apartments in 1975.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-Keuffel-65)

In 1975, the western part of the [Keuffel and Esser Manufacturing Complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keuffel_and_Esser_Manufacturing_Complex "Keuffel and Esser Manufacturing Complex") (known as "Clock Towers") was converted into residential apartments, after having been an architectural, engineering and drafting facility from 1907 to 1968;[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-Keuffel-65) the eastern part portion became residential apartments in 1984 (now called the _Grand Adams_).[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-Keuffel-65)

#### Waterfront

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hoboken,_New_Jersey&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Waterfront")]

The [Hudson Waterfront](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson_Waterfront "Hudson Waterfront") defined Hoboken as an archetypal port town and powered its economy from the mid-19th to mid-20th century, by which time it had become essentially industrial (and mostly inaccessible to the general public). The large production plants of Lipton Tea and Maxwell House, and the [drydocks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drydock "Drydock") of [Bethlehem Shipbuilding Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bethlehem_Shipbuilding_Corporation "Bethlehem Shipbuilding Corporation") and [Todd Shipbuilding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Todd_Shipbuilding "Todd Shipbuilding") dominated the northern portion for many years. On June 30, 1900, [a large fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1900_Hoboken_Docks_Fire "1900 Hoboken Docks Fire") at the [Norddeutscher Lloyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norddeutscher_Lloyd "Norddeutscher Lloyd") piers killed numerous people and caused almost $10 million in damage.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-66)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-67) The southern portion (which had been a U.S. base of the [Hamburg-American Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamburg-American_Line "Hamburg-American Line")) was seized by the federal government under [eminent domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eminent_domain "Eminent domain") at the outbreak of [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I"), after which it became (with the rest of the Hudson County) a major East Coast cargo-shipping port.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

[![Image 31](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/50/Hoboken_December_2022.jpg/250px-Hoboken_December_2022.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hoboken_December_2022.jpg)

Pier A Park

With the development of the [Interstate Highway System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_Highway_System "Interstate Highway System") and [containerization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Containerization "Containerization") shipping facilities (particularly at [Port Newark-Elizabeth Marine Terminal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Newark-Elizabeth_Marine_Terminal "Port Newark-Elizabeth Marine Terminal")), the docks became obsolete, and by the 1970s were more or less abandoned.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-Hoboken_Museum-38) A large swath of River Street, known as the [Barbary Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbary_Coast "Barbary Coast") for its taverns and boarding houses (which had been home for many dockworkers, sailors, merchant mariners, and other seamen) was leveled as part of an [urban renewal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_renewal "Urban renewal") project. Though control of the confiscated area had been returned to the city in the 1950s, complex lease agreements with the [Port Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Authority "Port Authority") gave it little influence on its management. In the 1980s, the waterfront dominated Hoboken politics, with various civic groups and the city government engaging in sometimes nasty, sometimes absurd politics and court cases. By the 1990s, agreements were made with the [Port Authority of New York and New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Authority_of_New_York_and_New_Jersey "Port Authority of New York and New Jersey"), various levels of government, Hoboken citizens, and private developers to build commercial and residential buildings and "open spaces" (mostly along the bulkhead and on the foundation of un-utilized [Pier A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landmarks_of_Hoboken,_New_Jersey "Landmarks of Hoboken, New Jersey")).[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-68)

The northern portion, which had remained in private hands, has also been re-developed. While most of the dry-dock and production facilities[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-69)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-70) were razed to make way for mid-rise apartment houses, many sold as investment condominiums, some buildings were renovated for adaptive re-use (notably the Tea Building, formerly home to Lipton Tea,[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-71) and the Machine Shop, home of the Hoboken Historic Museum).[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-72) Zoning requires that new construction follow the street grid and limits the height of new construction to retain the architectural character of the city and open sight-lines to the river. Downtown, [Frank Sinatra Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Sinatra_Park "Frank Sinatra Park") and [Sinatra Drive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinatra_Drive?action=edit&redlink=1 "Sinatra Drive (page does not exist)") honor the man most consider to be Hoboken's most famous son, while uptown the name Maxwell recalls the factory with its smell of roasting coffee wafting over town and its huge neon "Good to the Last Drop" sign, so long a part of the landscape. The midtown section is dominated by the [serpentine rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serpentine_rock "Serpentine rock") outcropping atop of which sits Stevens Institute of Technology (which also owns some, as yet, undeveloped land on the river). At the foot of the cliff is [Sybil's Cave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sybil's_Cave "Sybil's Cave") (where 19th century day-trippers once came to "take the waters" from a natural spring), long sealed shut, though plans for its restoration are in place. The promenade along the river bank is part of the [Hudson River Waterfront Walkway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson_River_Waterfront_Walkway "Hudson River Waterfront Walkway"), a state-mandated master plan to connect the municipalities from the [Bayonne Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayonne_Bridge "Bayonne Bridge") to [George Washington Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington_Bridge "George Washington Bridge") and provide contiguous unhindered access to the water's edge and to create an urban linear park offering expansive views of the Hudson with the spectacular backdrop of the New York skyline. As of 2017, the city was considering using [eminent domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eminent_domain "Eminent domain") to take over the last operating maritime industry in the city, the Union Dry Dock.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-73)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey#cite_note-74)
